strengths: The paper offers a useful empirical contribution: naturally authored multilingual captions can provide complementary visual information about the same images. This perspective is relevant to vision-language dataset construction and complements work focused on multilingual accessibility or benchmark performance.

The evidence spans human Crossmodal captions, two captioning systems, and Visual Genome grounding. Equal-caption-count model comparisons show gains in annotated-object coverage: Table 3 reports multilingual average recall of 11.5% versus 9.6% for English-only Vertex captions, and 12.0% versus 9.5% for LLaVA. This supports a substantive content difference beyond surface wording.

The separate human study provides useful corroboration. With 10 US English speakers and 10 Japanese speakers describing 30 images, multilingual unions contain 8.4% more objects, 7.7% more relations, and 6.5% more attributes than English-only unions (Appendix 8.3).

The manuscript makes meaningful efforts to validate its analysis, including a 15-speaker translation audit reporting mean quality of 4.68/5, translation-free embedding comparisons, and interpretable scene-graph examples. The distinction between semantic content and expressive variation is clearly motivated.
weaknesses: Experimental reporting contains consequential inconsistencies. Every entry in the LLaVA fine-tuning matrix in Table 14 matches the corresponding Vertex entry in Table 4, despite supposedly different training and evaluation captions. Also, Table 2 gives a Vertex monolingual attribute average of 1.98, although the listed values average approximately 1.69. These could be reporting mistakes, but the submitted evidence does not establish the claimed independent replication or reliable aggregate effect sizes.

Measurement validation is incomplete, especially for expressive variation. The translation audit in Appendix 8.1 evaluates model-generated captions and primarily checks semantic preservation; it does not establish that translation preserves the tone and authenticity measured by LIWC on human Crossmodal captions. The multilingual embedding check can retain language identity, and near-chance source-language prediction by one linear classifier does not exclude artifacts affecting other measurements. Scene-graph parsing and concept-merging accuracy are also not quantitatively validated.

The inference in Section 3.2 is unsupported: finding similar diversity across languages within one model and across different English-captioning models does not rule out language-conditioned operating modes. No theoretical or empirical bound establishes the assumed relationship between these quantities. Likewise, the human comparisons associate language with annotator population; they do not isolate language as the cause of different perceptual tendencies. The descriptive findings remain useful, but the proposed explanations are less secure.

The practical training implications exceed what is directly demonstrated. Fine-tuning and evaluating against captions from the same source language establishes reference-distribution matching, without establishing improved visual representations or robustness. Visual Genome grounding strengthens the coverage claim, but measures object recall without corresponding precision or grounding of added relations and attributes; more counted content therefore does not necessarily imply better overall caption quality.

Reproducibility and uncertainty reporting are insufficient: exact model checkpoints, decoding settings, fine-tuning hyperparameters, and concept-merging thresholds are not adequately specified, while the principal tables lack confidence intervals or repeated-run variability. Overall, the grounded coverage findings support a worthwhile contribution, but unresolved measurement validity and experimental reporting concerns place the manuscript near the acceptance boundary.
